name: Wasmi v2 (independent-suite evidence: wasmi-benchmarks)
baseline: WAMR fast-interpreter, Wasm3 and Wasmtime Pulley interpreter (execution); V8, Wasmtime (Winch, Cranelift) and Wasmer (Singlepass, Cranelift) (startup)
metric: throughput (execution geomean) and startup (compile plus instantiate geomean)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks: 21 execution test cases (counter loops, fibonacci, sort, prime sieve, matrix-mul, nbody, argon2, keccak, mandelbrot, spectralnorm, miniz compression, word-count, serde_json parse, regex-redux, bulk memory ops) and 7 startup test cases (bz2, pulldown-cmark, spidermonkey, ffmpeg, coremark, argon2, erc20), geometric mean per runtime.
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean, relative to the fastest runtime per test (lower is better), AMD EPYC 7763: Wasmi v2 eager x12.40 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51, Wasmtime Pulley x27.92 (derived from page data: 1.38x faster than WAMR, 1.33x than Wasm3, 2.25x than Pulley). Apple M2 Pro: x8.83 vs x14.77, x12.64, x29.80 (1.67x, 1.43x, 3.37x derived). Apple M4 Pro: x8.06 vs x18.64, x10.71, x23.97 (2.31x, 1.33x, 2.97x derived). Intel i7700: x6.60 vs x11.11, x8.50, x24.08 (1.68x, 1.29x, 3.65x derived). Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C: x8.36 vs x12.43, x11.95, x23.70 (1.49x, 1.43x, 2.84x derived); Wasmi v2 eager is also 1.6x, 1.9x and 2.4x faster than Wasmi 1.0 eager on EPYC (x19.56), M4 Pro (x15.66) and i7700 (x16.09) (derived from page data). Startup geomean (EPYC): Wasmi v2 lazy-unchecked x1.04 and lazy x1.37 vs V8 x33.27, Wasmer Singlepass x162.12, Wasmtime Winch x298.15, Wasmer Cranelift x1484.15, Wasmtime Cranelift x1634.19, WAMR x56.73; Wasmi v2 eager x38.88 is not faster than V8 on EPYC (x33.27) but is on the Xeon (x22.62 vs x29.21). Startup numbers at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-startup.svg
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks (Rust edition 2024, criterion): [profile.bench] lto=fat, codegen-units=1; Rust-based benchmark inputs built with [profile.wasm] opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. Runtime versions pinned in the suite: wasmi v2 = v2.0.0-beta.7, wasmi v1 = 1.0.9. rustc version and the C compiler flags used for wasm3 and WAMR are not stated in the README.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (primary, numbers quoted), Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (the five machine folders of wasmi-benchmarks-plots/data; geomean plots read for every machine)
tradeoffs: Interpreter: steady-state execution is about 10x behind optimising JITs, so the win is over other interpreters and in startup (lazy compilation), not over Wasmtime Cranelift or V8 peak speed. Lazy modes defer compile and validation cost to first call ('lazy.unchecked' also skips validation, which is only safe for trusted modules). Pure safe-ish Rust, no_std friendly, runs where JITs cannot (iOS, embedded, wasm itself).
caveats: Suite and plots are run by the Wasmi maintainers (first-party for Wasmi, but code, flags and CPU models are public so tier A applies). Plot values are 'relative time vs. optimal runtime' (geometric mean over test cases of the ratio to the fastest runtime on each case, lower is better), read from the SVG text of the geomean plots, not from a table; run dates are not stated on the plots (suite commits date from Aug-Sep 2026). Not every runtime runs every test case (support matrix in the README), so geomeans cover each runtime's runnable cases. wasm3 needs a C compiler with musttail support; wasm3, WAMR and wasmedge are built through the suite's own build scripts, so their optimisation flags are the suite's choice. Interpreters are 5-12x behind the best JITs (V8 x1.05, Wasmtime Cranelift x1.15, Wasmer Cranelift x1.17 on EPYC) in steady-state execution. Wasmi v2 in the suite is v2.0.0-beta.7; Wasmi 2.0.0 was prepared for release on 2026-09-01 (commit 'Prepare Wasmi v2.0.0 release'). On the Apple M4 Pro and Intel i7700 plots the rows are labelled 'Wasmi 2.0 (eager)' etc. Flagged is_evidence_for_known: Wasmi is already catalogued, this adds the multi-machine third-party-style suite as evidence.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'WebAssembly AOT compiler or JIT github README benchmark vs wasmtime wasmer startup compile time speedup' surfaced wasmi-benchmarks; opened its README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks/HEAD/README.md) and the wasmi-benchmarks-plots data folders (amd-epyc-7763, apple-m2-pro, apple-m4-pro, intel-i7700, intel-xeon-platinum-8573c).

name: Silverfir-nano (independent-suite evidence: wasmi-benchmarks)
baseline: Wasm3 and WAMR fast-interpreter (interpreter mode); Wasmtime Winch and Wasmer Singlepass baseline JITs, plus Wasmtime Cranelift and V8 (JIT mode, Apple silicon only)
workload: Same wasmi-benchmarks execution and startup geomean as the Wasmi v2 entry: 21 execution cases and 7 startup cases.
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test (lower is better). Interpreter: EPYC 7763 x9.02 vs Wasm3 x16.51 and WAMR x17.07 (1.83x, 1.89x derived from page data); Apple M2 Pro x6.30 vs x12.64, x14.77 (2.01x, 2.34x); Apple M4 Pro x5.97 vs x10.71, x18.64 (1.79x, 3.12x); Intel i7700 x5.56 vs x8.50, x11.11 (1.53x, 2.00x); Xeon 8573C x7.01 vs x11.95, x12.43 (1.70x, 1.77x). JIT: EPYC x1.25 vs Wasmtime Winch x2.35 and Wasmer Singlepass x2.95 (1.88x, 2.36x derived); M2 Pro x1.06 vs x3.12, x4.60; M4 Pro x1.07 vs x3.17, x4.85. On Apple silicon the JIT also edges Wasmtime Cranelift (x1.27 M2 Pro, x1.31 M4 Pro) and V8 (x1.22, x1.19); on x86 it is slower than Cranelift (EPYC x1.25 vs x1.15, i7700 x1.46 vs x1.25, Xeon x1.28 vs x1.21).
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks (Rust edition 2024, criterion): [profile.bench] lto=fat, codegen-units=1; Rust-based benchmark inputs built with [profile.wasm] opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. Runtime versions pinned in the suite: wasmi v2 = v2.0.0-beta.7, wasmi v1 = 1.0.9. rustc version and the C compiler flags used for wasm3 and WAMR are not stated in the README.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (primary, numbers quoted), Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (the five machine folders of wasmi-benchmarks-plots/data; geomean plots read for every machine)
tradeoffs: Startup is the cost: the JIT's startup geomean is x926.77 on EPYC (x628-x927 on all machines) vs Wasmtime Winch x298.15 and Wasmer Singlepass x162.12, and the interpreter's startup (x61.98) is slightly behind Wasm3 eager (x51.60) and WAMR (x56.73). JIT targets x86-64 and AArch64 only; the project is young (69 stars).
caveats: Suite and plots are run by the Wasmi maintainers (first-party for Wasmi, but code, flags and CPU models are public so tier A applies). Plot values are 'relative time vs. optimal runtime' (geometric mean over test cases of the ratio to the fastest runtime on each case, lower is better), read from the SVG text of the geomean plots, not from a table; run dates are not stated on the plots (suite commits date from Aug-Sep 2026). Not every runtime runs every test case (support matrix in the README), so geomeans cover each runtime's runnable cases. wasm3 needs a C compiler with musttail support; wasm3, WAMR and wasmedge are built through the suite's own build scripts, so their optimisation flags are the suite's choice. Interpreters are 5-12x behind the best JITs (V8 x1.05, Wasmtime Cranelift x1.15, Wasmer Cranelift x1.17 on EPYC) in steady-state execution. Silverfir-nano's own README reports Apple M4 only and links a 21-engine report on github.io (blocked here, not opened). Flagged is_evidence_for_known: the project is already catalogued; this is the multi-machine suite run by the Wasmi maintainers, which is a competitor of the project.
found_via: GitHub: wasmi-benchmarks README runtime table (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks/HEAD/README.md), then the wasmi-benchmarks-plots geomean SVGs for five machines; project README opened at github.com/mbbill/Silverfir-nano.

name: Stitch (independent-suite evidence: wasmi-benchmarks)
metric: throughput (execution geomean); startup roughly 4x better than eager Wasm3 but worse than lazy Wasm3
workload: Same wasmi-benchmarks execution and startup geomean as the Wasmi v2 entry (Stitch row 'Stitch (lazy)'; it cannot run the reverse-complement execution case).
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test (lower is better), Stitch (lazy) vs Wasm3 (eager) vs WAMR fast-interpreter: EPYC 7763 x15.73 vs x16.51 vs x17.07; Apple M2 Pro x11.94 vs x12.64 vs x14.77; Apple M4 Pro x9.70 vs x10.71 vs x18.64; Intel i7700 x8.11 vs x8.50 vs x11.11; Xeon 8573C x10.92 vs x11.95 vs x12.43. Derived from page data: 5-10% faster than Wasm3 and 8-92% faster than WAMR depending on machine. Startup (EPYC): Stitch lazy x11.68 vs Wasm3 eager x51.60 and WAMR x56.73, but Wasm3 lazy is x2.77.
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks (Rust edition 2024, criterion): [profile.bench] lto=fat, codegen-units=1; Rust-based benchmark inputs built with [profile.wasm] opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. Runtime versions pinned in the suite: wasmi v2 = v2.0.0-beta.7, wasmi v1 = 1.0.9. rustc version and the C compiler flags used for wasm3 and WAMR are not stated in the README. The suite's Cargo.toml notes opt-level=2 is required for the Stitch runtime's LLVM sibling-call optimisation.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (primary, numbers quoted), Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (the five machine folders of wasmi-benchmarks-plots/data; geomean plots read for every machine)
tradeoffs: Margin over Wasm3 is small (about 5-10%) and Wasmi v2 and Silverfir-nano now beat it; relies on guaranteed tail-call codegen (LLVM sibling calls need optimisation on); experimental project, README's own Coremark table shows Wasmtime 4-8x faster.
caveats: Suite and plots are run by the Wasmi maintainers (first-party for Wasmi, but code, flags and CPU models are public so tier A applies). Plot values are 'relative time vs. optimal runtime' (geometric mean over test cases of the ratio to the fastest runtime on each case, lower is better), read from the SVG text of the geomean plots, not from a table; run dates are not stated on the plots (suite commits date from Aug-Sep 2026). Not every runtime runs every test case (support matrix in the README), so geomeans cover each runtime's runnable cases. wasm3 needs a C compiler with musttail support; wasm3, WAMR and wasmedge are built through the suite's own build scripts, so their optimisation flags are the suite's choice. Interpreters are 5-12x behind the best JITs (V8 x1.05, Wasmtime Cranelift x1.15, Wasmer Cranelift x1.17 on EPYC) in steady-state execution. Stitch's own README (first-party, Coremark on M2 Pro, Xeon E3, i9-13900K) says 'slightly faster on Mac, slightly slower on Linux, significantly faster on Windows' than Wasm3; the suite data show a consistent small lead on five machines. Last commit is 10.7 months old, close to the 12-month 'active' limit. Flagged is_evidence_for_known: Stitch is already catalogued.
found_via: GitHub: wasmi-benchmarks README runtime table (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks/HEAD/README.md) and the five wasmi-benchmarks-plots geomean SVGs; project README opened at github.com/makepad/stitch.
